В силу этого в ряде случаев ударение играет фонематическую роль, ср.: алма́ ‘яблоко’, и а́лма ‘не бери’. new_statements.translation: Stress in all content (autosemantic) words is dynamic (expiratory) and falls on the last syllable of the word. Only particles, postpositions and the negation affix are unstressed. Because of this, stress in a number of cases plays a phonemic role, cf. almá 'apple' vs. álma 'don't take'. In words extended by a series of affixes there may be two stresses, cf. menémcäsenä́ 'in my opinion, as I suppose'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is dynamic and word-final in all content words of Azov Urum; enclitic particles, postpositions and the verbal negation suffix -ma do not take stress, so stress stays on the syllable before the negation suffix, yielding surface minimal pairs (almá 'apple' vs álma 'do not take').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Long polymorphemic words may carry two stresses (example menémcäsenä́ with a stress on the stem-final syllable and on the word-final syllable); no further rule given.
new_statements.exceptions: Unstressed: particles, postpositions, the negation affix (pre-stressing). No mention of loanwords, interrogatives or other lexical exceptions in this short (scheme-IV) article.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement for citation forms across all Azov Urum dialect groups (Kipchak, mixed, Oghuz); nothing on phrase-level prosody.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source (Muratov 1997) describes North-Azovian (Mariupol/Donetsk-oblast) Urum, the language of the Turkic-speaking 'Mariupol Greeks' resettled from Crimea in 1778-79, with Kipchak, mixed and Oghuz village dialects — this is what Glottolog 5.1's languoid 'Kipchak Urum' [urum1249, ISO uum, classified under Crimean Kipchak] denotes, and it is also the object of Garkavets 1999/2000, Smolina 2008, Tekin 2007 and Uyanik 2010. The target record's coordinates (42.04, 43.99, Georgia) and the earlier scan's named source (Skopeteas et al., Urum documentation project) instead concern Caucasian (Tsalka/Trialeti) Urum of Georgia, an Anatolian-Turkish-based variety of Pontic-Greek-origin speakers that Skopeteas explicitly distinguishes from Crimean/Azov Urum; statements about one variety should not be transferred to the other. Muratov's statement is for Azov Urum as a whole (all dialect groups), not a single village dialect.

tone_statements.citation: Skopeteas, Stavros. 2024. Post-predicate prosody in OV languages. In: Geoffrey Haig, Mohammad Rasekh-Mahand, Donald Stilo, Laurentia Schreiber & Nils N. Schiborr (eds.), Post-predicate elements in the Western Asian Transition Zone: A corpus-based approach to areal typology, 87-117. Berlin: Language Science Press. DOI 10.5281/zenodo.14266335
tone_statements.quote: Similarly to Turkish, prenuclear phrases are realized with rising contours delimited by a low target at their left edge and a high target at their right edge (φ L...Hφ ). A falling pitch accent (H*+L) appears in the stressed syllable in nuclear φ-phrases or when the word stress precedes the final syllable (e.g., in case of compounds or unstressed enclitics); cf. Kamali (2011: 93), Güneş (2013), Féry (2018: 250–257). In Figure 4/Left Panel, a high phrase tone (Hφ ) separates the preverbal focus from the preceding material; the focus is marked with a falling accent (H*+L), while the postnuclear domain (the verb) is de-accented.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 98-99, §5 'Narrow focus', paragraph introducing Caucasian Urum, with Figure 4 and example (7)
tone_statements.summary: No lexical tone; final word stress; post-lexical intonation of the Turkish type: phrase edge tones L..H on prenuclear φ-phrases, nuclear falling pitch accent H*+L on the stressed syllable (L* on a clause-final postverbal focus), de-accenting after the nucleus, L% at the ι-phrase end.
